analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour in two steps.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.15 an hour never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage in two steps: to $5.65 an hour starting July 2001, and to $6.15 an hour starting July 2002 [S2][S3]. At the time the minimum wage was $5.15 an hour, where it had been since 1997 [S2][S3]. A single representative introduced it; no other member signed on [S4]. It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before that Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, workers paid the federal minimum of $5.15 an hour would have gotten a raise to $5.65 and then $6.15 an hour — roughly a 19% increase over two years [S2][S3]. The lowest-paid workers in restaurants, retail, and other service jobs would have gained the most.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour in the year starting July 1, 2001, and to $6.15 an hour starting July 1, 2002 — about a 19% total increase [S2][S3].
The wage floor had been frozen at $5.15 since September 1997, so the bill would have restored some of the ground lost to inflation for the lowest-paid workers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, and other businesses that rely on low-wage labor — would bear the cost of the higher wage. Some of that cost can be passed to customers through prices, and some economists argue a higher minimum can reduce hiring for entry-level jobs.

drawbacks.text: Businesses that employ minimum-wage workers would face higher labor costs, which can show up as higher prices, reduced hours, or fewer entry-level positions — the standard objection to any minimum-wage increase.
A 19% increase over two years would have hit small businesses and low-margin industries like restaurants at the same time, with no phase-in flexibility beyond the two fixed dates in the bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A straightforward wage increase with no special carve-outs. The benefit to low-wage workers is direct and certain; the cost is spread across employers and consumers of minimum-wage industries. The main design weakness is the fixed two-step schedule, which pays no attention to economic conditions in 2002. On balance it transfers income from employers and customers to the lowest-paid workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant introduced the bill on June 19, 2001, with no cosponsors [S4][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which holds jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act [S5].
On August 20, 2001, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action followed; the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that pay the $5.15 minimum wage kept a wage floor that had been frozen since 1997 and was eroding with inflation. Low-wage workers gained nothing; the federal minimum did not rise during the 107th Congress.

for.name: Rep. James Traficant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; pursued no other recorded action and attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: Workforce Protections Subcommittee
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its August 2001 referral and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no coalition formed and no votes were ever recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Minimum-wage employers (restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses)
industries.note: Because the bill died, these employers kept the $5.15 wage floor set in 1997 rather than paying the $6.15 rate the bill would have required. Their savings came directly out of the paychecks of the lowest-wage workers.
